Authorities said the man's son reported him missing about noon Tuesday. Police told KDLH they found bare footprints leading 190 feet away from the man's home. For Tony Williams, the temperature in Minneapolis, Minnesota, was more than his body could handle. After shoveling outside his home without gloves for 45 minutes in minus-17-degree weather, Williams suffered second-degree frostbite, according to CNN affiliate KARE-TV. "On his finger pads, all of his fingers and his thumb, he had the formation of blisters," Dr. Cheryl Adkinson, an emergency physician at Hennepin County Medical Center who treated Williams, told KARE. In Grand Forks, North Dakota, the weather was severe enough to break a record temperature from 1979, with minus 37 degrees, according to the National Weather Service. The blast of cold, snow and ice wreaked havoc on traffic throughout the Midwest. The weather system, known as an "Alberta clipper," is expected to bring gusty winds, plummeting temperatures and a couple of inches of snow to Chicago, Illinois, on Wednesday morning, according to the weather service. The cold system from Canada will meet a system that originated in the Arctic and will spread below-freezing temperatures across the Great Lakes area, according to CNN meteorologist Guillermo Arduino.  See the forecast » . The system will bring many states in the Midwest the coldest days of the season, with hazardous wind chills. The weather service forecasters predicted snowfall of 1 to 5 inches from the Dakotas to the southern Great Lakes and even to the Northeast by the end of the week. "Near-whiteout conditions and slick roads are expected to impact travel of all types," according to the weather service's central region headquarters. After previous blasts of snow and cold, airports in Chicago, Minneapolis, Milwaukee, Wisconsin; and Grand Rapids and Detroit, Michigan, are expected to have continuing delays, Arduino said. Temperatures in Detroit are expected to reach minus 18 degrees Wednesday and minus 12 degrees Thursday. (CNN) — Parts of the upper Midwest were pounded Tuesday by fierce winds and dangerously low temperatures, giving several states their coldest conditions in decades. The bitter front swept through the upper Midwest and Great Lakes shortly after a blizzard struck the Northern Plains.

Minneapolis, Minnesota, recorded a temperature of minus 18 degrees Fahrenheit. In Hayward, Wisconsin, a sleepwalking-prone man died after being exposed to the frigid weather, CNN affiliate KDLH-TV in Duluth, Minnesota, reported. Authorities said his son notified them at about noon Tuesday that the man was missing. Police later discovered barefoot tracks extending 190 feet from his house, they told KDLH.

The Minneapolis cold also proved too much for Tony Williams. According to CNN affiliate KARE-TV, Williams developed second-degree frostbite after spending 45 minutes shoveling outside his home without gloves in minus-17-degree temperatures.

Dr. Cheryl Adkinson, the Hennepin County Medical Center emergency physician who treated him, told KARE that blisters had formed on the pads of every finger and on his thumb.

In Grand Forks, North Dakota, the temperature fell to minus 37 degrees, surpassing a record set in 1979, according to the National Weather Service.

Snow, ice and extreme cold caused widespread transportation problems throughout the Midwest. Schools and businesses closed in cities across the region, while residents worked to clear buried vehicles and streets. CNN’s iReport.com asked people to share how the winter weather was affecting them.

Railroad employee Matt Tesh experienced the painful near-zero wind chills firsthand Tuesday morning while clearing snow from tracks in Arlington Heights, Illinois, CNN affiliate WGN reported. Although he wore multiple layers beneath a vivid orange coat, he initially attempted to work without covering his face. He quickly changed his mind.

“Two or three minutes [without it], and my face was burning,” Tesh told WGN. CNN also provided images showing the storm’s effects in Chicago, Illinois.

Forecasters expected little improvement over the following several days. The National Weather Service said an “Alberta clipper” would reach Chicago on Wednesday morning, bringing strong wind gusts, sharply falling temperatures and a few inches of snow.

CNN meteorologist Guillermo Arduino said the Canadian cold front would collide with another system originating in the Arctic, spreading subfreezing conditions throughout the Great Lakes region. CNN also made the forecast available to readers.

The system was expected to produce the season’s coldest days in many Midwestern states, along with dangerous wind chills. By week’s end, National Weather Service forecasters anticipated 1 to 5 inches of snow from the Dakotas through the southern Great Lakes and into the Northeast.

“Near-whiteout conditions and slick roads are expected to impact travel of all types,” the weather service’s central region headquarters warned.

Arduino said earlier rounds of snow and cold would contribute to continued delays at airports in Chicago; Minneapolis; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; and the Michigan cities of Grand Rapids and Detroit.

Detroit was forecast to reach minus 18 degrees Wednesday and minus 12 degrees Thursday. Minneapolis was expected to fall to minus 21 Wednesday and minus 29 Thursday.

In Bismarck, North Dakota, Wednesday’s temperature was predicted to approach minus 20 degrees, with wind chills dropping as low as minus 45. Forecasters said another 3 to 6 inches of snow could fall there over the next several days, adding to the 5 inches left by the previous winter storm.

Forecasters urged residents to remain indoors, carry emergency supplies when traveling and check on older adults and neighbors without reliable heat.

Hospitals across the region reported treating dozens of people for cold-related injuries, including frostbite and hypothermia. Several patients suffered severe frostbite after spending prolonged periods outdoors or becoming stranded in disabled vehicles, health officials said.

Amtrak reported delays on several Midwest routes, while some transit agencies warned that frozen switches and equipment problems could affect commuter service.

Officials in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan closed stretches of highway because of crashes, drifting snow and near-whiteout conditions. Tow-truck operators were also forced to suspend service in some areas because wind chills made roadside work too dangerous.

Many school districts canceled classes or shifted to remote learning. Warming centers opened in major cities, including Chicago, Milwaukee and Minneapolis, with outreach teams distributing blankets and transporting people experiencing homelessness to shelters.

The coldest conditions are expected to persist through Wednesday morning. Temperatures should begin a gradual recovery later in the week, but forecasters said much of the region will remain below freezing through Friday.

Another round of snow could move across the Great Lakes toward the weekend, with lake-effect bands potentially producing locally heavy accumulations in western Michigan and areas east of Lakes Erie and Ontario.

Residents were advised to limit time outdoors, dress in multiple layers and keep pets inside. Officials also warned against using ovens, grills or generators indoors because of the risk of fire and carbon monoxide poisoning.

# Alberta clipper sweeps across Upper Midwest, bringing dangerous wind chills and hazardous snow

**MINNEAPOLIS —** A fast-moving Alberta clipper is driving a surge of Arctic air across the northern United States, threatening Minnesota, Wisconsin, Illinois, Michigan and North Dakota with dangerous wind chills, periods of snow and a rapid drop to below-freezing temperatures.

The storm’s relatively modest snowfall could still create serious travel problems because of gusty winds, rapidly falling temperatures and pockets of blowing snow. Roads that are initially wet or slushy may freeze quickly, producing difficult-to-detect patches of black ice during the evening and morning commutes.

The most severe cold is expected across North Dakota, Minnesota and northern Wisconsin, where wind chills could fall to dangerous levels—potentially tens of degrees below zero in exposed locations. Frostbite can develop on uncovered skin in a short time under those conditions.

Farther south and east, including northern Illinois and Michigan, temperatures are forecast to plunge below freezing as the clipper passes. Snow showers and squalls may briefly reduce visibility, while lake-enhanced bands could increase accumulations in parts of Michigan and areas near Lake Superior.

## State-by-state impacts

### North Dakota
North Dakota is on the leading edge of the Arctic air mass and faces some of the harshest wind chills. Even where snowfall remains limited, strong winds may blow loose snow across highways and reduce visibility in open country.

Residents are being urged to limit prolonged outdoor exposure, carry winter survival supplies and ensure livestock and outdoor animals have adequate shelter. Motorists traveling through rural areas should be prepared for rapidly changing conditions and long distances between services.

### Minnesota
Minnesota could see a combination of accumulating snow, gusty northwest winds and sharply falling temperatures. Travel conditions may deteriorate quickly, particularly in western, central and northern sections of the state.

The Twin Cities region may experience slick roads and reduced visibility during heavier snow showers. In northern Minnesota, bitter wind chills could create an immediate risk of frostbite and hypothermia, especially overnight and during the early morning.

### Wisconsin
Snow is expected to spread across Wisconsin as colder air pours into the state. Northern and western areas face the greatest danger from low wind chills, while central and southern Wisconsin may contend with icy roads as temperatures fall.

Near Lake Superior, localized lake enhancement could produce heavier snow. Gusty winds may also cause drifting on exposed roads and in rural areas.

### Illinois
Northern Illinois, including the Chicago area, could experience snow showers, falling temperatures and a rapid freeze. Even light accumulations may disrupt travel if snow melts on treated or heavily traveled roads and then refreezes.

Strong winds may make temperatures feel substantially colder than thermometer readings. Bridges, ramps and overpasses will be especially vulnerable to icing.

### Michigan
Michigan could face the longest period of snow because of additional moisture from the Great Lakes. Lake-effect or lake-enhanced bands may produce highly variable conditions, with relatively clear weather in one community and near-whiteout conditions only a short distance away.

The Upper Peninsula and northern Lower Peninsula are most vulnerable to heavier localized snow and dangerous wind chills. Western Michigan could also see persistent snow bands after the clipper’s main area of snow moves away.

## Why a small storm can cause major problems

Alberta clippers are compact, fast-moving systems that form near the Canadian Rockies and race southeast across the northern Plains and Great Lakes. They generally carry less moisture than major winter storms, but they can produce abrupt weather changes.

Their primary hazards often include:

- Bursts of snow that sharply reduce visibility  
- Strong northwest winds and blowing snow  
- Rapid temperature drops and flash freezing  
- Dangerous wind chills behind the system  
- Lake-effect snow after the main storm departs  

Because clippers move quickly, conditions can worsen with little warning. A short snow squall can make a highway temporarily impassable even when total accumulation is low.

## Safety concerns

Officials advise residents to avoid unnecessary travel during the worst conditions and to check the latest National Weather Service alerts before leaving home. Drivers should slow down, increase following distance and avoid cruise control on snow- or ice-covered roads.

Emergency kits should include blankets, warm clothing, water, food, medication, a flashlight, a phone charger, an ice scraper and jumper cables. Anyone who becomes stranded should generally remain with the vehicle unless safe shelter is clearly visible nearby.

People going outdoors should wear multiple loose-fitting layers and cover exposed skin. Warning signs of frostbite include numbness and pale, waxy or hardened skin. Hypothermia can cause intense shivering, confusion, slurred speech and loss of coordination.

Homeowners should also protect exposed pipes, check heating systems and use space heaters only with proper clearance from combustible materials. Generators and grills must never be operated indoors or in enclosed garages because of the risk of carbon-monoxide poisoning.

Forecast snowfall, wind and temperature details can vary significantly over short distances. Residents across the five-state region should monitor local forecasts, road-condition reports and updated winter weather advisories as the clipper moves through.

**By CNN Weather**

A blast of Arctic air has plunged much of the Upper Midwest into its coldest weather in decades, closing schools, disrupting travel and raising fears of frostbite and hypothermia.

Temperatures fell well below zero across Minnesota, Wisconsin, Illinois and North Dakota, while strong winds pushed wind chills to life-threatening levels. In some communities, exposed skin could develop frostbite in as little as 10 minutes, forecasters warned.

The National Weather Service urged residents to stay indoors whenever possible, keep emergency supplies in their vehicles and check on older adults, neighbors and people without reliable heat.

In **Minneapolis**, residents awoke to temperatures approaching 30 degrees below zero, with even colder wind chills. CNN affiliate **WCCO** reported that transit agencies and outreach workers were taking additional steps to protect commuters and people experiencing homelessness. Schools and businesses across the Twin Cities canceled classes or adjusted hours as officials warned that even brief exposure could be dangerous.

The deep freeze was equally severe in northern Wisconsin. In **Hayward**, temperatures sank into the 30s below zero, according to affiliate reports. Vehicles struggled to start, and ice crystals hung in the air as residents bundled in layers to complete essential errands. Local officials asked people to avoid unnecessary travel and to carry blankets, food and a fully charged phone if they had to drive.

Near Chicago, the Arctic outbreak brought conditions rarely experienced in the region. In **Arlington Heights, Illinois**, residents faced subzero temperatures and dangerously low wind chills. CNN affiliate **WLS** reported widespread school closures and delays, while rail and road crews worked to keep transportation systems operating. The extreme cold also increased the risk of frozen pipes and heating-system failures.

Farther northwest, **Grand Forks, North Dakota**, endured some of the harshest conditions. CNN affiliate **WDAZ** reported temperatures around 30 degrees below zero, with wind chills falling far lower. Officials warned that stranded motorists could quickly face a life-threatening emergency and advised drivers to postpone travel when possible.

The cold is being driven by a surge of air from the Arctic that has settled across the central United States. Although frigid winter weather is common in the Upper Midwest, the intensity and duration of this outbreak could challenge long-standing daily records in several cities.

Forecasters said some moderation is expected, but temperatures will remain dangerously low in many areas before warmer air arrives.

Residents should limit time outside, wear several loose layers, cover their face and hands, and bring pets indoors. Anyone showing signs of hypothermia — including confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness or uncontrollable shivering — should seek immediate medical help.
